title: Free RAM not released to OS after heavy dataframe operations
body:
### Description

I work on latest Ubuntu linux (24.04.2 LTS, but prev versions suffer from the same) and latest Polars (1.30).
I start with a dataframe of size of 10Gb, and perform a lot of groupby, join, math operations.
As a result, I end up having a 100Gb final dataframe that is returned from a python function that does all the processing. 

However, OS shows that 1TB of RAM is used.
I found [this ](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/76061800/polars-df-takes-up-lots-of-ram) explanation from Ritchie that "3x a table size is actually pretty good". However, not x10, right? Especially if we are talking about 0.9Tb wasted.

But the more, the merrier. If I proceed with computing more columns, this is the last row from my log file:
_**RSS=2766.6 GB**, sys RAM available=2543.5 GB, df size=**296.8 GB**._

And on the next operation process simply OOMs, 'cause total RAM size of the node is 2.9Tb.
Real data size is 300GB though.

Whatever I tried: calling malloc_trim(0) from within my Python process, running process with jemalloc allocator - this changes nothing, no effect whatsoever.

AI suggested this:

> 
> Why malloc_trim(0) and jemalloc don’t work from Python with Polars
> ❌ Why malloc_trim(0) from Python doesn't work:
> Polars is written in Rust, and compiled Rust code by default uses libc::malloc, not Python's malloc or the heap that Python controls.
> 
> So when you call malloc_trim(0) in Python, it only affects the memory allocated via Python’s own malloc (e.g., NumPy, lists, etc.), not memory allocated inside Polars (Rust).
> 
> The memory bloat you’re seeing is likely entirely in Rust’s heap, managed separately.
> 
> ❌ Why jemalloc via LD_PRELOAD didn't help:
> LD_PRELOAD only affects dynamically-linked binaries.
> 
> Many Rust programs — including Polars and Arrow components — are compiled with --release and statically link to the default system allocator.
> 
> So jemalloc never got used by the Rust part, even though you preloaded it.


✅ Why doing it from within Rust could help
> Yes — calling malloc_trim(0) or linking jemalloc from within the Rust side of Polars can work, but only if Polars is explicitly built to use jemalloc or invokes trimming from Rust
> 
> 🔧 What would work (on the Rust side):
> ✅ 1. Polars compiled with jemalloc as global allocator
> Inside Polars (or Arrow, or any Rust dependency handling large memory):
> 
> rust
> #[global_allocator]
> static GLOBAL: jemallocator::Jemalloc = jemallocator::Jemalloc;
> ✅ Effect:
> 
> jemalloc returns memory to OS much more effectively than glibc.
> 
> This will solve fragmentation and memory hoarding issues if jemalloc is actually linked and used.
> 
> ✅ 2. Call malloc_trim(0) from Rust directly
> If sticking with glibc, add in Rust:
> 
> rust
> extern "C" {
>     fn malloc_trim(pad: usize) -> i32;
> }
> unsafe {
>     malloc_trim(0);
> }
> This will work because:
> 
> It's executed from within the same allocator and heap as the Rust code that allocated the memory.
> 
> But:
> 
> glibc still doesn’t return memory unless fragmentation conditions are met.
> 
> So this is hit-or-miss, unlike jemalloc which is much more consistent.

 ✅ Concrete Path Forward
> Best option:
> Have the Polars Rust code base expose an optional jemalloc feature, or at least support compiling with:
> 
> bash
> RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native" cargo build --release --features jemalloc
> And inside Polars:
> 
> rust
> #[cfg(feature = "jemalloc")]
> #[global_allocator]
> static GLOBAL: jemallocator::Jemalloc = jemallocator::Jemalloc;

I'm not an expert in C, Rust, Linux kernels or allocators. But this simply feels wrong. Please, if some measures from described above can be taken, let's optionally take them. For the God's sake, please implement them. What kind of high perf, big data number crunching engine is this if it handles memory so inefficiently?

Maybe there is some known workaround? I've asked in discord, to no avail.

But I am sharing the workaround I found that works for Windows. You can simply call
```python

def trim_windows_process_memory(pid: int = None) -> bool:
    """Causes effect similar to malloc_trim on -nix."""

    # Define SIZE_T based on the platform (32-bit or 64-bit)
    if ctypes.sizeof(ctypes.c_void_p) == 4:
        SIZE_T = ctypes.c_uint32
    else:
        SIZE_T = ctypes.c_uint64

    # Get a handle to the current process
    if not pid:
        pid = ctypes.windll.kernel32.GetCurrentProcess()

    # Define argument and return types for SetProcessWorkingSetSizeEx
    ctypes.windll.kernel32.SetProcessWorkingSetSizeEx.argtypes = [
        ctypes.wintypes.HANDLE,  # Process handle
        SIZE_T,  # Minimum working set size
        SIZE_T,  # Maximum working set size
        ctypes.wintypes.DWORD,  # Flags
    ]
    ctypes.windll.kernel32.SetProcessWorkingSetSizeEx.restype = ctypes.wintypes.BOOL

    # Define constants for SetProcessWorkingSetSizeEx
    QUOTA_LIMITS_HARDWS_MIN_DISABLE = 0x00000002

    # Attempt to set the working set size
    result = ctypes.windll.kernel32.SetProcessWorkingSetSizeEx(pid, SIZE_T(-1), SIZE_T(-1), QUOTA_LIMITS_HARDWS_MIN_DISABLE)

    if result == 0:
        # Retrieve the error code
        error_code = ctypes.windll.kernel32.GetLastError()
        logger.error(f"SetProcessWorkingSetSizeEx failed with error code: {error_code}")
        return False
    else:
        return True
```

after heavy operations, along with gc.collect() that releases unused RAM to OS with no problems. However, Windows not always can be used due to a plethora of reasons. I hope to find some clean solution for Linux as well.

I have a similar problem, I failed to free the occupied memory after a cross join even when using the garbage collector, I attached a minimal example:

- Linux 5.15.0-1075-aws
- Python 3.11.3
- polars 1.29.0

```
import polars as pl
import psutil
import time

def get_memory_info():
    """Get current memory usage info"""
    process = psutil.Process()
    memory_info = process.memory_info()
    return memory_info.rss / 1024**3  # Convert to GB

def create_large_dataframe(size_mb=5000):
    """Create a large dataframe for testing"""
    n_rows = size_mb * 1000  # Approximate rows for target size
    
    df = pl.DataFrame({
        'id': range(n_rows),
        'group': [f'group_{i % 100}' for i in range(n_rows)],
        'value1': [i * 1.5 for i in range(n_rows)],
        'value2': [i * 2.3 for i in range(n_rows)],
        'value3': [i * 0.7 for i in range(n_rows)],
        'category': [f'cat_{i % 50}' for i in range(n_rows)]
    })
    
    return df

def heavy_operations(df):
    """Perform heavy operations that cause memory bloat"""
    print(f"Initial memory: {get_memory_info():.2f} GB")
    print(f"Initial dataframe size: {df.estimated_size('mb')} MB")
    
    # Create smaller dataframes for cross join
    df_small1 = df.head(10000).select(['id', 'group', 'value1'])
    df_small2 = df.head(5000).select(['category', 'value2', 'value3'])
    
    print(f"Small df1 size: {df_small1.estimated_size('mb')} MB")
    print(f"Small df2 size: {df_small2.estimated_size('mb')} MB")
    print(f"Before cross join - Memory: {get_memory_info():.2f} GB")
    
    # Cross join - this should cause massive memory bloat
    df_cross = df_small1.join(df_small2, how='cross')
    
    print(f"After cross join - Memory: {get_memory_info():.2f} GB")
    print(f"Cross joined dataframe size: {df_cross.estimated_size('mb')} MB")
    print(f"Cross join result rows: {df_cross.height}")
    
    # Additional operations on the cross joined data
    df_processed = df_cross.with_columns([
        (pl.col('value1') * pl.col('value2')).alias('product'),
        (pl.col('value1') + pl.col('value3')).alias('sum_val'),
        pl.col('group').str.len_chars().alias('group_len')
    ])
    
    print(f"After processing cross join - Memory: {get_memory_info():.2f} GB")
    print(f"Processed dataframe size: {df_processed.estimated_size('mb')} MB")
    
    # Group the cross joined data
    df_final = df_processed.group_by(['group', 'category']).agg([
        pl.col('product').mean().alias('avg_product'),
        pl.col('sum_val').sum().alias('total_sum'),
        pl.col('id').count().alias('count')
    ])
    
    print(f"After final groupby - Memory: {get_memory_info():.2f} GB")
    print(f"Final dataframe size: {df_final.estimated_size('mb')} MB")
    
    return df_final

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("Starting Polars memory reproduction test...")
    print(f"Available system memory: {psutil.virtual_memory().total / 1024**3:.2f} GB")
    
    # Create initial dataframe
    initial_memory = get_memory_info()
    print(f"Baseline memory: {initial_memory:.2f} GB")
    
    # Create large dataframe
    df = create_large_dataframe(size_mb=5000)  # Start with 5GB dataframe
    
    # Perform heavy operations
    df_result = heavy_operations(df)
    
    final_memory = get_memory_info()
    memory_bloat = final_memory - initial_memory
    df_size_gb = df_result.estimated_size('mb') / 1024
    
    print(f"\n=== RESULTS ===")
    print(f"Final memory usage: {final_memory:.2f} GB")
    print(f"Memory bloat: {memory_bloat:.2f} GB")
    print(f"Actual dataframe size: {df_size_gb:.2f} GB")
    print(f"Memory overhead ratio: {memory_bloat / df_size_gb:.1f}x")
```

Let's put it to the extreme:
```

    df_small1 = df.head(50000).select(['id', 'group', 'value1'])
    df_small2 = df.head(30000).select(['category', 'value2', 'value3'])
```

```python
    df_result = heavy_operations(df)

    del df_result
    del df

    final_memory = get_memory_info()
    memory_bloat = final_memory - initial_memory   
    
    print(f"\n=== RESULTS ===")
```

i get this:

So RAM is kept occupied even when the dataframes themselves are deleted and garbage collected. That's just absurd. And the more operations you do (groupby, math, joins), the more this bloat grows. But never decreases, until it OOMs the process.

By definition, this kind of program behaviour is a memory leak.

comments.author: ritchie46
comments.body:
> So RAM is kept occupied even when the dataframes themselves are deleted and garbage collected. That's just absurd. And the more operations you do (groupby, math, joins), the more this bloat grows. But never decreases, until it OOMs the process.

That's not how memory allocators work. They keep memory around for later usage. I ran your example in a for loop and memory usage saturates. It doesn't leak, but the memory allocator keeps it assigned to the process. This is normal. 

See: https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/issues/9225

comments.author: Pneirz
comments.body:
Thanks for the reply. I understand that allocators like glibc::malloc keep memory reserved for future use, and that this behavior isn’t considered a memory leak in a strict sense. Still, when working in real environments like shared clusters or containerized systems, it becomes a problem if hundreds of gigabytes stay allocated even after all DataFrames are dropped and garbage collection is triggered. From the system’s point of view, that memory is unavailable, and it doesn’t help much that the allocator plans to reuse it eventually.

One of the core ideas behind Polars, as described in the documentation, is efficient memory usage for large-scale data processing. But in practice, this kind of behavior feels like a contradiction. Would it be possible to expose a method like pl.trim_memory() that internally calls malloc_trim(0) from Rust, or at least to provide clearer support for compiling with jemalloc? I think many of us would benefit from having that level of control, especially when working with limited or shared resources. Other tools like pandas and Arrow already offer ways to manage memory more explicitly, so having something similar in Polars would make a big difference.

> > So RAM is kept occupied even when the dataframes themselves are deleted and garbage collected. That's just absurd. And the more operations you do (groupby, math, joins), the more this bloat grows. But never decreases, until it OOMs the process.

That particular example might be not OOMing if you repeat calling the same transformations on the same data. In that case I really observed high, but constant RAM usage.

However, in real applications one wants to apply different transformations, and what's where it OOMs in practice.

I would not post this issue if it would not lead to real OOMs. I also hoped that "on memory pressure" allocator will eventually return unused RAM back to os, but that's not happening.

I am running into OOMs on Ubuntu because of exactly this behaviour of the allocator.

My goal is to prepare a ML featureset from raw time series using 4 python functions/transformations.
Each one accepts polars dataframe from the previous "stage", enriches it with its own aggregates, and returns original dataframe enriched  with new features.

As mentioned in the start of topic, each successive transformation after returning of enriched dataframe adds up to the memory bloat up to 10 times of that new dataframe size. System counts that "bloat" memory as "available", but not "free".

On some of the 4 transformations, process OOMs. What's remarkable, if I restart process and load last known dataframe **from disk,** there is of course no such terabyte size bloat, and that **transformation works succesfully.** 

This is a clear evidence that such memory bloat is real and preventing system from working normally, that it's leading to real OOMs.

If you are not convinced, I can work on a reproducer with a series of similar transforms that OOMs while having a dataframe of relatively small size compared to the total RAM.

In fact, persisting every intermediate transformation to disk in a child process, killing it and reading in another process is the only workaround I found on Ubuntu so far. But I can't call it neither convenient nor performant, as in my case persisting of a large dataset to SSD takes up to 50 minutes each time. And even with this workaround, I can't fully solve my task, as at the final stage dataframe is created, but memory bloat is so high that operation of saving to parquet is OOMing.

comments.author: ritchie46
comments.body:
A memory allocator cannot return the mwmory to the OS because it is fragmented. You can try tune jemallocs settings to better suit your needs. But note that it isn't a choice. 

We have a confirmed leak that might cause this fragmentation. That will be resolved next release. But if it still happens after that it is likely because of memory fragmentation at the allocator. A query engine is process will do a lot of memory allocations and thus will lead to eventual memory fragmentation.

You can run the queries in another process if it remains a problem.

comments.author: fingoldo
comments.body:
Ok. "Good news, everyone" )

I did not know Polars is already using jemalloc.
At first I was going to try building polars from source with different JEMALLOC_SYS_WITH_MALLOC_CONF params.

However, I was lucky to find [this](https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/blob/main/py-polars/polars/__init__.py):
```python

    jemalloc_conf = "dirty_decay_ms:500,muzzy_decay_ms:-1"
    if os.environ.get("POLARS_THP") == "1":
        jemalloc_conf += ",thp:always,metadata_thp:always"
    if override := os.environ.get("_RJEM_MALLOC_CONF"):
        jemalloc_conf += "," + override
    os.environ["_RJEM_MALLOC_CONF"] = jemalloc_conf
```

So, basically, what we've been asking for is already there!! We can tune all jemalloc settings without re-building polars, just by setting that _RJEM_MALLOC_CONF. @coastalwhite can you confirm please this env var is not going anywhere? maybe it makes sense to document it, along with the fact that polars uses jemalloc (via tikv-jemallocator)?

But wait a second. What's that **hardcoded muzzy_decay_ms:-1 for?!**

> In jemalloc, memory goes through multiple stages:
> 
> Active – currently in use.
> 
> Dirty – freed but not yet zeroed; can be reused by the program.
> 
> Muzzy – freed and zeroed, but not yet returned to the OS.
> 
> Returned – truly unmapped (returned to the OS).

**Consequence of muzzy_decay_ms:-1**

Jemalloc never releases zeroed (muzzy) memory to the OS.
Your memory usage will plateau but never drop, even after you delete big DataFrames and call gc.collect().
You may observe high resident set size (RSS) in htop, even when Python's heap is mostly empty.
**That's why Polars seems to never release memory, even after garbage collection.**

Let's quickly check it.

I'm running the same [test ](https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/issues/23128#issuecomment-2969506905) with 200 GB bloat never released to OS, even after dataframe deletion and garbage collection:

```
export _RJEM_MALLOC_CONF="muzzy_decay_ms:0"
python test.py
```

> 
> Starting Polars memory reproduction test...
> Available system memory: 2975.25 GB
> Baseline memory: 0.04 GB
> Initial memory: 3.03 GB
> Initial dataframe size: 2179.1458129882812 MB
> Small df1 size: 1.1396408081054688 MB
> Small df2 size: 0.6237030029296875 MB
> Before cross join - Memory: 3.04 GB
> After cross join - Memory: 92.44 GB
> Cross joined dataframe size: 65374.37438964844 MB
> Cross join result rows: 1500000000
> After processing cross join - Memory: 120.38 GB
> Processed dataframe size: 93984.60388183594 MB
> After final groupby - Memory: 124.08 GB
> Final dataframe size: 0.16069412231445312 MB
> 
> === RESULTS ===
> Final memory usage: 0.07 GB
> Memory bloat: 0.03 GB
> Actual dataframe size: 0.00 GB
> Memory overhead ratio: 174.1x

Behold! RAM is freed and returned to OS!!!

@Pneirz you are welcome to run your real workloads with muzzy_decay_ms:0 or any additional settings Ritchie [referenced ](https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/issues/23128#issuecomment-2975286250)(narenas:1,dirty_decay_ms:0,muzzy_decay_ms:0,background_thread:true come to mind), I will do the same and report here.
Maybe we can figure out optimal jemalloc options together.
I think we are finally getting somewhere with this problem!

@ritchie46 @coastalwhite is there any particular reason that we are using muzzy_decay_ms:-1?

Polars, and Pandas to that extent, often require more RAM than the final result occupies, that's normal. They need extra RAM to do the interim joins etc. What you can do is to try a different execution engine, i've been told Streaming one will become a primary & most efficient. you can try it already with `collect(engine="streaming")`.

comments.author: bneijt
comments.body:
I ran into this issue, and turns out it was actually a configuration on our end. I was running Polars in an AWS Fargate task and although the [task had a limit](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/task_definition_parameters.html#task_size), the container itself executing did [not have a memory limit set](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/task_definition_parameters.html#standard_container_definition_params).

A job that used to crash on anything less than 60GB of memory, now executed on 8GB limit without issue. My guess is that because the container did not have any ulimit set, jemalloc does not detect a limit and keeps allocating till the OOM hits.

comments.author: rgeronimi
comments.body: This is an issue for our production small servers where Polars shine - these servers allocate memory that is unreleased, thus making it difficult for us to track correctly the memory usage on a complex python stack of third party libs. Having the ability to release memory would greatly simplify our use case

comments.author: sylvlecl
comments.body:
Ran into the same issue in our web app, you may revert to a more eager purge behaviour by setting your own jemalloc settings through environment variable `_RJEM_MALLOC_CONF`, for example:
` _RJEM_MALLOC_CONF=background_thread:true,muzzy_decay_ms:0`

Be aware though that for some operations on large arrays you may have slowdowns like identified in https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/issues/18088#issuecomment-2277968519 .

This behaviour comes from that "feature" of jemalloc  [5.2.0](https://github.com/jemalloc/jemalloc/releases/tag/5.2.0), which causes page faults for large allocations:
> Implement opt.oversize_threshold which uses a dedicated arena for requests crossing the threshold, also eagerly purges the oversize extents. Default the threshold to 8 MiB. (@interwq)

So allocations larger than 8Mb are always eagerly purged. 
This is supposed to be configurable through the option "oversize_threshold", but seems like there is a bug:
https://github.com/jemalloc/jemalloc/issues/2824
muzzy_decay_ms=-1 disables that behaviour, which is documented nowhere.

Finally, in the dev branch of jemalloc, this behaviour has been changed, so in a future release we may benefit from both the memory release and the "correct" performances:
https://github.com/jemalloc/jemalloc/pull/2466 

Hoping that those behaviours will be better documented and configurable now that commitment to improve jemalloc has been renewed!

comments.author: matteocoletta
comments.body:
I ran into the same issue on a Gentoo server — Polars would allocate memory during a .collect() on an aggregated LazyFrame and not release it afterwards.

What worked for me was launching IPython with the following jemalloc tuning:

`env _RJEM_MALLOC_CONF='abort_conf:true,background_thread:true,dirty_decay_ms:0,muzzy_decay_ms:0' ipython`

Benchmark on the same query, using Polars v1.40.1:

- Without the config: the query allocates up to ~20 GB during .collect(), with ~14 GB still held after the result is materialized, and only released after terminating ipython.
- With the config: the query allocates up to ~5 GB, dropping to ~2 GB after .collect() returns. The remaining ~2 GB matches the size of the resulting DataFrame (held by IPython's output cache regardless of whether the result was assigned to a variable).

Thanks for all the useful suggestions in this thread!

comments.author: komodovaran
comments.body:
I ran the quite complex benchmark mentioned here: https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/issues/22871, though with rows slightly dialed down to avoid swapping on my MacBook. For good measure, I'd highly suggest using `spawn`-ed subprocesses to clear out leftover memory after doing all your computations. Otherwise, you _will_ be stuck with zombie memory regardless of the env fix. In Kubernetes, spawning a subprocess to do the computations is perfectly fine, in my experience. I'm not quite sure what's going on with 500k rows, but I'm guessing there must be some boundary conditions for when different caches kick in. In longer iterations the memory fix keeps the memory _completely_ flat, while it quite easily accumulates by default. In more simple benchmarks where IO/memory are more limiting factors the performance hit seems to be just ~10% or less, but the memory doesn't risk exploding. ``` =========================================================================== 🚀 Starting Scalability Benchmark (20 internal iterations per run) =========================================================================== 📊 Testing Dataset Size: 100,000 rows 🔹 Running WITHOUT memory fix... Finished | Avg Iter: 0.032s ± 0.003s | Peak Worker RSS: 1423.8 MB 🔸 Running WITH memory fix... Finished | Avg Iter: 0.037s ± 0.001s | Peak Worker RSS: 1038.1 MB 📈 Slowdown with memory fix: +16.37% 📊 Testing Dataset Size: 250,000 rows 🔹 Running WITHOUT memory fix... Finished | Avg Iter: 0.046s ± 0.003s | Peak Worker RSS: 3093.6 MB 🔸 Running WITH memory fix... Finished | Avg Iter: 0.060s ± 0.001s | Peak Worker RSS: 2368.4 MB 📈 Slowdown with memory fix: +30.81% 📊 Testing Dataset Size: 500,000 rows 🔹 Running WITHOUT memory fix... Finished | Avg Iter: 0.081s ± 0.010s | Peak Worker RSS: 3936.7 MB 🔸 Running WITH memory fix... Finished | Avg Iter: 0.108s ± 0.008s | Peak Worker RSS: 4579.4 MB 📈 Slowdown with memory fix: +33.49% 📊 Testing Dataset Size: 1,000,000 rows 🔹 Running WITHOUT memory fix... Finished | Avg Iter: 0.149s ± 0.002s | Peak Worker RSS: 4170.9 MB 🔸 Running WITH memory fix... Finished | Avg Iter: 0.181s ± 0.003s | Peak Worker RSS: 1374.8 MB 📈 Slowdown with memory fix: +21.44% ```
```python import math import os import statistics import subprocess import matplotlib.pyplot as plt DATASET_SIZES = [ 100_000, 250_000, 500_000, 1_000_000, ] ITERATIONS_PER_RUN = 20 CHILD_COMPLEX_CODE_TEMPLATE = """ import os import gc import time import numpy as np import polars as pl import psutil N_ROWS_MAIN = {size} N_ROWS_METRICS = {size} N_GROUPS = 1_000 N_TAG_COLS = 50 ITERATIONS = {iterations} def rss_mb() -> float: return psutil.Process(os.getpid()).memory_info().rss / 1024**2 def make_synthetic_data(): rng = np.random.default_rng(42) dates = np.arange( np.datetime64("2020-01-01"), np.datetime64("2020-01-01") + np.timedelta64(N_ROWS_MAIN, "s"), dtype="datetime64[ms]", )[:N_ROWS_MAIN] groups = rng.integers(0, N_GROUPS, size=N_ROWS_MAIN).astype(np.int32) dft = pl.DataFrame({ "group_id": groups, "Date": dates, "Value1_original": rng.normal(50, 10, N_ROWS_MAIN).astype(np.float64), "AlarmLevel4_original": rng.normal(80, 5, N_ROWS_MAIN).astype(np.float64), }) metrics_vib = pl.DataFrame({ "group_id": rng.integers(0, N_GROUPS, size=N_ROWS_METRICS).astype(np.int32), "Date": np.sort(rng.choice(dates, size=N_ROWS_METRICS, replace=True)), "distance": rng.exponential(1.0, N_ROWS_METRICS).astype(np.float64), "threshold_used": rng.uniform(1.5, 3.0, N_ROWS_METRICS).astype(np.float64), "is_outlier_Value1": rng.choice([True, False], size=N_ROWS_METRICS, p=[0.05, 0.95]), }) tag_cols = {f"temp_{i}": rng.normal(0, 1, N_ROWS_MAIN).astype(np.float64) for i in range(N_TAG_COLS)} tag_cols["Date"] = dates tags = pl.DataFrame(tag_cols) wide_cols = {"Date": dates[:N_ROWS_METRICS]} for i in range(N_TAG_COLS): wide_cols[f"dist_temp_{i}"] = rng.exponential(1.0, N_ROWS_METRICS).astype(np.float64) wide_cols[f"thr_temp_{i}"] = rng.uniform(1.5, 3.0, N_ROWS_METRICS).astype(np.float64) metrics_wide = pl.DataFrame(wide_cols) return dft, metrics_vib, tags, metrics_wide def build_vib_pipeline(dft_lazy, metrics_lazy): joined = dft_lazy.join(metrics_lazy, on=["group_id", "Date"], how="left") return joined.with_columns([ ((pl.col("distance") > pl.col("threshold_used")) & (~pl.col("is_outlier_Value1"))) .fill_null(False) .alias("anomaly_kmeans"), ((pl.col("Value1_original") > pl.col("AlarmLevel4_original")) & (pl.col("AlarmLevel4_original").is_not_null())) .fill_null(False) .cast(pl.Boolean) .alias("accident"), ]).with_columns([ (pl.col("anomaly_kmeans") | pl.col("is_outlier_Value1")) .fill_null(False) .cast(pl.Boolean) .alias("anomaly_Value1"), ]) def build_tag_pipeline(tag_lazy, metrics_lazy, targets): processed = tag_lazy.join(metrics_lazy, on="Date", how="left") expressions = [] drops = [] for col in targets: dc, tc = f"dist_{col}", f"thr_{col}" drops.extend([dc, tc]) cond = (pl.col(dc) > pl.col(tc)) & (pl.col(dc).is_not_null()) expressions.append(pl.when(cond).then(1).otherwise(0).alias(f"anomaly_{col}")) return processed.with_columns(expressions).drop(drops) def run_once(dft, metrics_vib, tags, metrics_wide, tag_targets): pipes = [ build_vib_pipeline(dft.lazy(), metrics_vib.lazy()), build_tag_pipeline(tags.lazy(), metrics_wide.lazy(), tag_targets), ] with pl.StringCache(): results = pl.collect_all(pipes, streaming=True) del results gc.collect() dft, metrics_vib, tags, metrics_wide = make_synthetic_data() tag_targets = [f"temp_{i}" for i in range(N_TAG_COLS)] for i in range(1, ITERATIONS + 1): t0 = time.perf_counter() run_once(dft, metrics_vib, tags, metrics_wide, tag_targets) elapsed = time.perf_counter() - t0 print(f"ITER_METRICS|{i}|{rss_mb():.1f}|{elapsed:.4f}") """ def execute_worker(size, iterations, use_fix): current_env = os.environ.copy() if use_fix: current_env["_RJEM_MALLOC_CONF"] = "abort_conf:true,dirty_decay_ms:0,muzzy_decay_ms:0" else: current_env.pop("_RJEM_MALLOC_CONF", None) worker_code = CHILD_COMPLEX_CODE_TEMPLATE.replace("{size}", str(size)).replace("{iterations}", str(iterations)) process = subprocess.Popen( ["uv", "run", "--with", "psutil", "python", "-c", worker_code], env=current_env, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE, text=True, ) durations = [] peak_mem = 0.0 while True: line = process.stdout.readline() if not line and process.poll() is not None: break if line.strip().startswith("ITER_METRICS|"): _, _, mem_val, time_val = line.strip().split("|") peak_mem = max(peak_mem, float(mem_val)) durations.append(float(time_val)) process.wait() mean_time = statistics.mean(durations) if durations else 0.0 if len(durations) > 1: std_time = statistics.stdev(durations) sem_time = std_time / math.sqrt(len(durations)) else: sem_time = 0.0 return mean_time, sem_time, peak_mem def run_scaling_benchmark(): means_without_fix = [] stds_without_fix = [] means_with_fix = [] stds_with_fix = [] print("===========================================================================") print(f"🚀 Starting Scalability Benchmark ({ITERATIONS_PER_RUN} internal iterations per run)") print("===========================================================================") for size in DATASET_SIZES: print(f"\n📊 Testing Dataset Size: {size:,} rows") print(" 🔹 Running WITHOUT memory fix...") mean_no_fix, std_no_fix, peak_no_fix = execute_worker(size, ITERATIONS_PER_RUN, use_fix=False) means_without_fix.append(mean_no_fix) stds_without_fix.append(std_no_fix) print( f" Finished | Avg Iter: {mean_no_fix:.3f}s ± {std_no_fix:.3f}s | Peak Worker RSS: {peak_no_fix:.1f} MB" ) print(" 🔸 Running WITH memory fix...") mean_with_fix, std_with_fix, peak_with_fix = execute_worker(size, ITERATIONS_PER_RUN, use_fix=True) means_with_fix.append(mean_with_fix) stds_with_fix.append(std_with_fix) print( f" Finished | Avg Iter: {mean_with_fix:.3f}s ± {std_with_fix:.3f}s | Peak Worker RSS: {peak_with_fix:.1f} MB" ) slowdown_pct = ((mean_with_fix - mean_no_fix) / mean_no_fix) * 100 if mean_no_fix > 0 else 0.0 print(f" 📈 Slowdown with memory fix: {slowdown_pct:+.2f}%") plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6)) plt.errorbar( DATASET_SIZES, means_without_fix, yerr=stds_without_fix, label="Default (Without Memory Fix)", marker="o", color="crimson", linewidth=2, capsize=5, elinewidth=1.5, ) plt.errorbar( DATASET_SIZES, means_with_fix, yerr=stds_with_fix, label="Optimized (With Decay Fix)", marker="s", color="dodgerblue", linewidth=2, linestyle="--", capsize=5, elinewidth=1.5, ) plt.title( "Processing Speed Scaling Performance (With SEM Error Bars)", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", pad=15, ) plt.xlabel("Dataset Size (Number of Rows)", fontsize=11, labelpad=10) plt.ylabel("Average Execution Time per Iteration (Seconds)", fontsize=11, labelpad=10) plt.grid(True, linestyle=":", alpha=0.6) plt.xticks(DATASET_SIZES, [f"{x:,}" for x in DATASET_SIZES]) plt.legend(fontsize=11, loc="upper left") output_plot = "processing_speed_scaling.png" plt.savefig(output_plot, dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight") print("\n" + "=" * 75) print(f"🏁 Benchmark Complete. Scaling plot exported cleanly to: {output_plot}") print("=" * 75) if __name__ == "__main__": run_scaling_benchmark() ```
